target: AG1’s claim that AI improves society by making life, work, learning, accessibility, and safety better
objection: AI is not reliably net-positive because, in real deployments, it tends to harm economic well-being by replacing or downgrading human labor, weaken critical thinking by encouraging people to outsource reasoning, reproduce and amplify racial discrimination, and create serious privacy/surveillance risks.

target: AG2’s assumption that AI harms are systematically inevitable and therefore prevent any reliable net-positive social impact
objection: The harms cited by the opponent are not inevitable; they depend heavily on deployment choices and governance. Bias can be reduced with audits, fairness constraints, better data, and human review; privacy risks can be limited with data minimization and privacy-preserving methods; educational misuse can be designed to force engagement; and economic harms can be mitigated with reskilling and augmentation-focused deployment.

target: AG1’s claim that AI broadly improves work, learning, safety, and accessibility
objection: AI’s main practical effects are often concentrated among model owners while workers face lower bargaining power and job insecurity. Tools that summarize or tutor also encourage outsourcing reasoning, and AI systems trained on historical data can reproduce discrimination and privacy-invasive surveillance, so the benefits do not reliably outweigh the harms.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s negative effects are the typical outcome and cannot be reliably avoided
objection: The opponent treats harms like labor displacement, weak critical thinking, bias, and surveillance as unavoidable, but those outcomes are contingent on implementation choices. With worker reskilling, verification-focused education design, fairness auditing, and privacy-preserving data practices, AI can be used as augmentation rather than replacement and can be net-positive.

target: AG1’s general optimism that AI reliably benefits society despite common tradeoffs
objection: In common deployments, AI’s practical effects routinely include recurring harms: automation reduces job security and wages, drafting/summarizing tools weaken independent reasoning, assistive systems still rely on sensitive data and profiling, and safety-monitoring tools introduce surveillance and overreliance. These harms make the claim of reliable net social benefit unjustified.

target: AG2’s assumption that AI benefits cannot be achieved without recurring structural harms that cancel them out
objection: The harms are contingent, not inevitable. AI can be deployed to augment jobs instead of replacing them, to require reasoning and citations in education, to reduce bias through representative data and auditing, and to protect privacy through minimization and access controls; therefore the opponent’s blanket pessimism is undermined.

target: AG1’s claim that AI reliably improves daily life, learning, work, accessibility, and safety
objection: Even in everyday life and health, AI can be miscalibrated or opaque and worsen decisions; in learning and work it can weaken reasoning and verification habits; in accessibility it can come with privacy and autonomy losses; and in safety it can create surveillance, false positives, and unclear accountability. These recurring tradeoffs undermine the claim of reliable net benefit.

target: AG2’s assumption that AI deployments usually lack safeguards and therefore produce unavoidable harms
objection: Many harms the opponent cites are not inherent to AI but depend on deployment choices. Human-in-the-loop decision policies, calibration, documentation, fallback procedures, data minimization, consent controls, and privacy-preserving architectures can make systems auditable, safer, and less privacy-invasive, so the claim that harms routinely dominate benefits is not dependable.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s benefits in convenience, learning, accessibility, and safety usually outweigh its downsides
objection: The same deployment patterns that create convenience and safety also often cause harms that negate them: miscalibrated decision support can worsen health outcomes, drafting and tutoring can reduce independent reasoning, accessibility tools can require sensitive data collection and profiling, and monitoring can create surveillance and overreliance. Because these harms are recurring, AI cannot be reliably described as good for society overall.

target: AG1’s broader support for AI as socially beneficial
objection: AI makes large-scale, highly convincing deception cheap, which increases impersonation, scams, verification burdens, and privacy/autonomy harms. It also undermines critical thinking because people must constantly verify authenticity in an environment full of synthetic text, voice, and video. These structural harms can outweigh the claimed convenience and productivity benefits.

target: AG2’s claim that cheap AI-generated deception makes society worse overall
objection: AI also makes defenses against deception cheaper and more effective. It can detect deepfakes, spot suspicious patterns, speed up fraud response, and improve identity verification, shifting verification from constant manual checking to targeted automated triage and reducing scam harm rather than letting it dominate.

target: AG1’s assumption that AI-enabled detection will scale well enough to offset deception
objection: Detection systems do not generalize reliably, produce false positives and false negatives, and can be outpaced by adversarial adaptation. Identity and risk-scoring tools also increase surveillance and friction. So the idea that automated defense will keep verification cheap and effective is not well-grounded.

target: AG2’s claim that deception harms outweigh AI’s benefits
objection: Even if AI makes forgeries easier, it simultaneously enables scalable defenses that reduce fraud and verification burden. Automated detection, anomaly spotting, and risk-aware authentication can preserve convenience while reducing successful scams, so the claimed dominance of deception harms is not necessary.

target: AG1’s assumption that AI defenses will reliably stay ahead of AI-generated fraud and keep verification costs low
objection: That assumption is weak because detection is probabilistic, attackers adapt in an arms race, and verification often requires surveillance-like data access. As a result, defense can become expensive, frictionful, and privacy-invasive rather than cheap and reliable.

target: AG2’s claim that cheap synthetic content necessarily makes AI socially harmful
objection: AI can reduce both the creation of deception and the success of deception by enabling automated detection, anomaly detection, and stronger identity workflows. That can shift verification from constant manual scrutiny to targeted checks and preserve convenience while improving security.

target: AG1’s assumption that AI defenses can keep up with AI-forged content without adding substantial cost or burden
objection: AI defenses are probabilistic, degrade under adversarial adaptation, and often require more monitoring, human review, appeals, and sensitive data collection. This creates more verification friction and privacy loss, so the claimed net benefit from defenses is not assured.

target: AG2’s claim that AI-generated deception will dominate AI’s social effects
objection: The same advances that make synthetic text, voice, and video cheaper also enable scalable countermeasures such as deepfake detection, anomaly spotting, liveness checks, and risk-aware authentication. These defenses can reduce fraud and verification burden enough that AI’s net social effect remains positive.

target: AG1’s assumption that AI defenses will reliably lower fraud and verification costs without new burdens
objection: Defense will not cleanly scale: detectors make mistakes, attackers can evade them, and effective verification often requires sensitive behavioral or biometric data. That means AI can create a new verification and surveillance burden instead of reducing it, so the net-positive tradeoff is not guaranteed.

target: AG2’s argument that cheap deception makes AI socially net-negative
objection: Cheap deception does not force a net-negative outcome because AI can also reduce fraud and verification burden through detection, anomaly spotting, and risk scoring. By filtering low-risk interactions and reserving manual checks for high-risk cases, AI can preserve convenience while improving security.
